pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Greenhouse Gas Science for ages 11–12 — WHY certain gases warm the planet, at the molecular level: short-wave solar in, long-wave infrared out, and the specific gases that trap the outgoing IR.
• Standards — UK: KS3 chemistry 'Earth and atmosphere' (composition of the atmosphere; carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases; human impacts) and KS3 physics 'Energy' / 'Waves' (the electromagnetic spectrum; infrared radiation). Builds toward GCSE combined-science climate content.
• Standards — US: NGSS MS-ESS3-5 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-5]) and MS-PS4-2 (waves; how the EM spectrum interacts with matter). DCI ESS3.D, PS4.B.
• Operational details: anchor on the two-radiation idea (Sun sends mostly visible/short-wave; Earth re-emits invisible thermal IR) BEFORE naming gases; use a photon-and-molecule model so 'trapping' is the molecule absorbing an IR photon and re-emitting in all directions, not a solid lid; contrast IR-active gases (CO2, CH4, H2O, N2O — three-or-more atoms, vibrations change the dipole moment) with IR-transparent N2/O2 (symmetric diatomics); layer in potency/GWP only after the mechanism is felt.
• Checkpoint: [Tier B] child can explain that the atmosphere is transparent to incoming sunlight but partly opaque to Earth's outgoing infrared, and that only certain molecules absorb that IR; [Tier C] child can say WHY (dipole-changing vibrations; symmetric diatomics don't absorb) and rank CO2 vs CH4 by concentration-vs-potency.
bestPractices: Separate the two radiations first: sunlight arrives mostly as short-wavelength visible/near-IR (~0.1–4 µm); Earth, being cool, re-radiates long-wavelength thermal infrared (~4–30 µm). The atmosphere treats these two bands completely differently — that asymmetry IS the greenhouse effect.

Model 'trapping' as absorb-and-re-emit-in-all-directions, not reflection off a barrier: a CO2 molecule catches an outgoing IR photon, jiggles, and re-emits — half of that goes back down. Repeated many times, this slows heat's escape and raises surface temperature.

Explicitly contrast IR-active vs IR-inactive molecules: gases with three or more atoms (CO2, CH4, H2O, N2O, O3) have vibrations that change the molecule's dipole moment and so absorb IR; symmetric diatomics N2 and O2 — 99% of the air — do not, which is why trace gases matter so much.

Distinguish the NATURAL greenhouse effect (keeps Earth ~+33 °C warmer; without any GHGs Earth's surface would average ≈ −18 °C / 255 K) from the ENHANCED effect (extra CO2/CH4 from burning fossil fuels and agriculture). The mechanism is good and necessary; the problem is the amplification.

Introduce potency vs abundance carefully: CH4 traps far more heat per molecule than CO2 but is present in much smaller amounts and is shorter-lived — use Global Warming Potential to compare fairly over a stated time horizon rather than saying one gas is simply 'worse'.
keyRepresentations: Photon-and-molecule diagram: incoming yellow short-wave arrows pass straight through the gas layer; outgoing red IR arrows get caught by CO2/CH4 molecules that vibrate and re-emit in all directions.

Two-band spectrum picture: the Sun's emission curve (peaking in visible) beside Earth's emission curve (peaking in thermal IR ~10 µm), with the atmospheric 'absorption bands' shaded to show where GHGs block outgoing IR (and the 8–15 µm atmospheric window where it escapes).
Molecular ball-and-spring models: symmetric O2/N2 stretching (no dipole change → IR-transparent) vs bending/asymmetric-stretch of CO2 (dipole change → IR-active).
GWP comparison bars: heat trapped per molecule (CH4 ≫ CO2) alongside atmospheric concentration (CO2 ≫ CH4), showing why both matter.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole — believing warming is caused by holes 'letting extra heat in'. These are distinct: ozone depletion is about UV and CFCs in the stratosphere; the greenhouse effect is about IR absorption by GHGs in the troposphere.
Thinking GHGs 'reflect' heat back like a mirror or form a solid 'blanket/lid'. The real mechanism is absorption and omnidirectional re-emission of infrared by individual molecules.
Assuming the most abundant gases (nitrogen, oxygen) must be the greenhouse gases. In fact N2 and O2 are IR-transparent; the trace gases (CO2 ~0.04%, CH4 far less) do the trapping.
Believing the greenhouse effect is inherently bad. The natural effect is essential for life; the concern is the human-caused ENHANCEMENT.
Treating 'CO2 is the problem' as the whole story and ignoring methane, or conversely thinking methane's higher potency makes CO2 unimportant — missing the concentration × potency × lifetime picture.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: understand WHY certain gases warm the planet at a molecular level. Separate the two radiations first (short-wave sunlight in, long-wave infrared out), model 'trapping' as a molecule absorbing an IR photon and re-emitting it in all directions (not a reflecting lid), contrast IR-active gases (CO2, CH4, H2O, N2O — three-or-more atoms whose vibrations change the dipole moment) with IR-transparent symmetric diatomics N2/O2, distinguish the natural greenhouse effect from the human-enhanced one, and compare gases by potency × abundance × lifetime. A causal photon-and-molecule investigation is proposed to lead; categorisation, dialogue, and reference diagrams consolidate. All activities are proposed, research-informed approaches whose effectiveness has not been validated.

activities.title: Photon-and-molecule energy-balance investigation
feedback: If a learner expects added N2/O2 to warm the surface: point out the outgoing IR photons passed straight through — symmetric diatomics have no dipole change when they vibrate, so they cannot absorb IR at all, not even 'a little'.

If a learner describes the molecule 'reflecting' or 'bouncing' the photon like a mirror: highlight that the molecule absorbs the photon, vibrates, then re-emits in a random direction — only some of that goes downward; it is absorb-and-re-emit, not reflection off a barrier.

If a learner thinks the gases trap incoming sunlight: replay the short-wave arrows passing through to the ground untouched, and contrast with the outgoing IR that gets caught — trapping acts on the OUTGOING infrared.

If a learner concludes CO2 at ~0.04% is too tiny to matter: show the thermometer climbing as a small number of CO2 molecules are added, and that stripping all GHGs drops the modelled surface toward 255 K.

If a learner says methane's higher potency makes CO2 unimportant (or vice versa): use the comparison mode to show that total effect depends on potency per molecule AND how many molecules are present AND how long each persists, compared over a stated GWP time horizon.

If a learner treats the ~+33 °C rise as the whole human problem: distinguish it from the smaller human-enhanced increment — the natural effect is essential; the concern is the extra warming humans add on top.
activities.rationale: The target understanding is a dynamic causal chain (photon absorbed → molecule vibrates → re-emitted in all directions → surface warms). This activity is a proposal designed so learners may grasp that chain more readily by driving the model and watching temperature respond than by reading an asserted outcome; its effectiveness has not been validated. Separating the two radiation bands before naming gases, and modelling trapping as omnidirectional re-emission, are intended to target the most common misconceptions.
sourceClaims: For a molecular vibration to absorb infrared energy the motion must change the molecule's dipole moment; all molecules with three or more atoms meet this criterion, while symmetric diatomics N2 and O2 (and monatomic Ar) do not absorb IR — so the trace gases CO2, H2O, CH4, N2O and O3 are the greenhouse-active constituents.

Incoming solar radiation is dominated by short wavelengths (~0.1–4 µm, peaking in the visible) while Earth re-radiates thermal infrared (~4–30 µm, peaking near 10 µm); the atmosphere is largely transparent to the incoming short-wave but absorbs much of the outgoing long-wave, with an 8–15 µm atmospheric window through which some IR escapes.

Without its greenhouse gases Earth's surface would average roughly 255 K (about −18 °C); the natural greenhouse effect raises it by about 33 °C to a habitable mean, and human emissions of CO2 and CH4 enhance this effect.
learnerActions: Start with air made only of N2 and O2: watch the Sun emit short-wave photons that pass straight through the gas layer and warm the ground, and watch the ground re-emit red infrared photons that escape to space while a surface thermometer sits low.

Drag a few CO2 molecules into the air and observe what happens when an outgoing IR photon meets one: the molecule bends/jiggles (its bonds flexing in a mode that changes its dipole) and re-emits the photon in a random direction — roughly half the time back toward the ground.
Add more CO2 (and try CH4, H2O) and record how the surface thermometer and an 'escaping to space' counter change.
Swap the added gas for extra N2 or O2 and note that outgoing IR passes through untouched — nothing changes.

Toggle 'strip all greenhouse gases' and observe the modelled surface temperature fall toward about 255 K (−18 °C); then toggle to air containing greenhouse gases and see it rise to a habitable mean (≈ 288 K / +15 °C). The ~+33 °C jump is the NATURAL greenhouse warming; present-day air carries this natural effect plus a smaller human-enhanced increment on top. Present all figures as model outputs, not precise measurements.

In a comparison mode, match a few CH4 molecules against many CO2 molecules to feel potency per molecule versus abundance; write one sentence explaining why both a highly potent trace gas and an abundant weaker one matter. Note the comparison depends on a stated GWP time horizon.
activities.intendedInsight: Warming happens because the atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming short-wave sunlight but partly opaque to Earth's outgoing infrared: only molecules whose vibrations change their dipole moment absorb and re-emit that IR (the main greenhouse gases CO2, CH4, N2O and H2O all have three or more atoms), sending some back down and slowing heat's escape. Symmetric N2/O2 — 99% of the air — do not absorb IR, which is why trace gases dominate the effect. The natural effect is essential; human emissions enhance it.

activities.title: Two-band spectrum and molecular-vibration reference
feedback: If a learner reads the bars as 'CH4 is simply worse than CO2': note that potency per kilogram (or per molecule) is only one axis; CO2's far larger concentration and emissions (and much longer persistence) mean it contributes more of the human-enhanced warming than CH4 — compare fairly using a stated GWP time horizon.
If a learner cannot locate where IR escapes: direct them to the 8–15 µm atmospheric window on the spectrum.
If a learner thinks all vibrations absorb IR: contrast the symmetric O2/N2 stretch (no dipole change) with CO2's bending mode.
activities.rationale: Static spectra, molecular models, and GWP bars name and consolidate the discriminations after the mechanism is felt. They assert relationships rather than letting the learner cause them, so they are proposed as reference companions rather than the primary route to the causal insight; a fixed diagram can still teach the relationships even though it cannot be manipulated.
sourceClaims: Incoming solar radiation is dominated by short wavelengths (~0.1–4 µm, peaking in the visible) while Earth re-radiates thermal infrared (~4–30 µm, peaking near 10 µm); the atmosphere is largely transparent to the incoming short-wave but absorbs much of the outgoing long-wave, with an 8–15 µm atmospheric window through which some IR escapes.

For a molecular vibration to absorb infrared energy the motion must change the molecule's dipole moment; all molecules with three or more atoms meet this criterion, while symmetric diatomics N2 and O2 (and monatomic Ar) do not absorb IR — so the trace gases CO2, H2O, CH4, N2O and O3 are the greenhouse-active constituents.
learnerActions: Study a two-band spectrum picture: the Sun's emission curve peaking in the visible beside Earth's emission curve peaking in the thermal IR near 10 µm, with atmospheric absorption bands shaded and the 8–15 µm window where IR escapes marked.
Use ball-and-spring molecular models to compare the symmetric stretch of O2/N2 (no dipole change → IR-transparent) with the bending and asymmetric stretch of CO2 (dipole change → IR-active).

Read GWP comparison bars showing warming per kilogram emitted over the stated time horizon (CH4 ≫ CO2) alongside atmospheric concentration (CO2 ≫ CH4), note the stated GWP time horizon, and explain in your own words why both gases matter.
Label a photon-and-molecule diagram: incoming short-wave arrows passing through, outgoing IR arrows caught by CO2/CH4 and re-emitted in all directions.
activities.intendedInsight: The asymmetry between how the atmosphere treats short-wave in and long-wave out is what produces the greenhouse effect, and it traces back to which molecular vibrations change the dipole moment. Potency and abundance are separate axes that must be combined (with lifetime) to judge a gas's overall contribution.

activities.title: 3D vibrational-mode inspector for CO2
feedback: If a learner assumes every vibration absorbs IR: show the symmetric stretch of CO2, whose dipole does not change, as a mode that does not absorb, contrasted with the bending mode that does.

If a learner thinks 3D viewing changes the planetary story: clarify that the whole-planet energy balance is a flat photons-in/photons-out flow; the 3D view adds detail at the single-molecule scale and complements rather than replaces the 2D account.
activities.rationale: A 3D molecule viewer offers a different view of the dipole-change idea than a flat ball-and-spring picture, since it can be rotated to show the bending motion in both perpendicular directions. It is proposed as a supplementary inspector; the planetary energy-balance story that carries the learning is conveyed clearly in 2D.
sourceClaims: For a molecular vibration to absorb infrared energy the motion must change the molecule's dipole moment; all molecules with three or more atoms meet this criterion, while symmetric diatomics N2 and O2 (and monatomic Ar) do not absorb IR — so the trace gases CO2, H2O, CH4, N2O and O3 are the greenhouse-active constituents.
learnerActions: Rotate and view a CO2 molecule in three dimensions to see its vibrational modes: symmetric and asymmetric stretch (atoms moving along the molecule's straight line) and bending (which can happen in two perpendicular directions).
Identify which modes change the molecule's dipole moment (and therefore absorb IR) and which do not.
Relate what you see back to why CO2 absorbs outgoing infrared while symmetric N2/O2 do not.
activities.intendedInsight: Viewing a molecule's vibrational modes in 3D shows how its atoms move, and only modes that change the dipole moment absorb infrared — making the abstract 'dipole change' criterion concrete.

activities.title: Sort, sequence and explain: consolidating the discriminations
feedback: If a learner sorts N2/O2 as IR-active: remind them symmetric diatomics have no dipole change on vibration and absorb no IR.

If a learner conflates greenhouse and ozone: ozone depletion is about CFCs destroying stratospheric ozone so more UV reaches the ground; the greenhouse effect is greenhouse gases absorbing outgoing IR, mostly in the lower atmosphere — different radiation and a different process (although CFCs and ozone are themselves also greenhouse gases).
If a learner orders the sequence with absorption on the incoming sunlight: the absorption step acts on the OUTGOING infrared from the surface.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, sequencing, and short-answer items are intended to help consolidate distinctions and surface residual misconceptions once the causal model is built. These recognition and recall formats can check understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent causal reasoning the investigation is intended to build, so they are best used as follow-up.
sourceClaims: For a molecular vibration to absorb infrared energy the motion must change the molecule's dipole moment; all molecules with three or more atoms meet this criterion, while symmetric diatomics N2 and O2 (and monatomic Ar) do not absorb IR — so the trace gases CO2, H2O, CH4, N2O and O3 are the greenhouse-active constituents.

Without its greenhouse gases Earth's surface would average roughly 255 K (about −18 °C); the natural greenhouse effect raises it by about 33 °C to a habitable mean, and human emissions of CO2 and CH4 enhance this effect.
learnerActions: Categorise gases as IR-active (CO2, CH4, H2O, N2O) or IR-transparent (N2, O2) and justify each placement by its molecular structure.

Put the mechanism in order: Sun → short-wave radiation → surface warms → emits infrared → infrared absorbed by GHG molecules → re-emitted in all directions → some returns to the surface → surface warms further (heat escapes to space more slowly).
Answer short questions: why do trace gases matter so much? how is the greenhouse effect different from the ozone hole? which radiation is actually trapped?
Estimate Earth's surface temperature with greenhouse gases versus with none, and explain the gap (≈ +33 °C natural effect; ≈ 255 K / −18 °C without GHGs, as modelled figures).
Distinguish the natural greenhouse effect from the enhanced effect and state what drives the enhancement (burning fossil fuels, agriculture).
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall and discrimination of the key categories, sequence, and distinctions: IR-active vs IR-transparent, incoming vs outgoing radiation, greenhouse vs ozone, natural vs enhanced.

activities.title: Ask-the-climate-scientist dialogue to untangle misconceptions
feedback: If the learner says N2/O2 trap 'a little' heat: steer them to the dipole-change criterion — symmetric diatomics do not absorb IR at all.
If the learner blames the ozone hole: separate the two — stratospheric UV/CFC chemistry versus tropospheric IR absorption.
If the learner treats water vapour as a direct human emission: discuss why its atmospheric amount responds to temperature, making it a feedback rather than a lever humans set directly.
activities.rationale: Dialogue suits a topic dense with persistent misconceptions because it lets learners voice and test their reasoning. It supports the mechanism rather than demonstrating it operating, so it is proposed as a follow-up to an investigation where the learner has already seen the process.
sourceClaims: Roughly 80% of students conflate the greenhouse effect with stratospheric ozone depletion, believing warming comes from 'holes letting heat in'; effective teaching explicitly separates the IR-absorption (troposphere) mechanism from UV/CFC ozone chemistry (stratosphere).
learnerActions: Pose the questions that puzzle you to a climate-scientist role (real teacher, peer-in-role, or a guided prompt), e.g. 'Why don't nitrogen and oxygen trap heat if they're 99% of the air?' and 'Isn't warming just the ozone hole letting heat in?'
Explain back, in your own words, why only certain molecules absorb IR and how greenhouse warming differs from ozone depletion.
Probe the follow-ups: is water vapour a human 'switch' like CO2 or a feedback? Is the greenhouse effect itself the problem, or its enhancement? What does 'potent' mean for methane?
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and defending the mechanism through dialogue can expose and help repair the misconception-heavy areas of this topic — abundance vs IR-activity, greenhouse vs ozone, natural vs enhanced, potency vs amount.

constraints: Establish the two-radiation asymmetry (short-wave in, long-wave IR out) BEFORE naming gases; layer in potency/GWP only after the absorb-and-re-emit mechanism is understood.
Model 'trapping' as a molecule absorbing an IR photon and re-emitting in all directions (so some returns toward the surface), not as reflection off a mirror or a solid blanket/lid.
Be explicit that N2 and O2 do not absorb IR at all (no dipole change on vibration) — avoid implying they trap heat 'just less' than CO2.

Distinguish the natural greenhouse effect (essential; ≈ +33 °C, surface ≈ 255 K without GHGs rising to ≈ 288 K/+15 °C) from the smaller human-enhanced increment; the mechanism is not inherently bad — the amplification is the concern.
Compare gases by potency per molecule AND concentration AND lifetime using a stated GWP time horizon; do not label one gas simply 'worse'.

Static spectra, GWP bars and labelled diagrams assert relationships and serve as references; they do not let the learner cause the process. Categorisation/sequence/short-answer formats consolidate and check discriminations but do not by themselves elicit independent causal construction.

The 3D vibrational-mode viewer and the live sim (dragging molecules, surface thermometer, escaping-to-space counter, GHG-strip toggle, GWP comparison mode) are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory tools; equivalent paper, ball-and-spring, or role-play versions can serve the same purpose.

Temperature values (255 K / −18 °C; +33 °C natural effect; ≈ 288 K/+15 °C habitable mean) are standard modelled figures from the cited energy-balance source; present them as model outputs, not precision measurements.
Efficacy of all activities here is untested; present them as proposed approaches using may/intended wording rather than as proven methods.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Several sources carry verified:false in the original row (UK KS3 curriculum statement, NGSS MS-ESS3-5/MS-PS4-2, and the '~80% of students conflate greenhouse with ozone' misconception statistic). The 80% figure (and its embedded 'effective teaching' assertion) and the standards mappings should be checked against primary sources before being cited as established.

The original framed a static image as able only to 'assert, not let the child cause' the mechanism and 3D as adding little; these have been softened to affordance/limit statements. A fixed diagram can still teach the relationships even though it cannot be manipulated.

The sim's binary toggle (no GHGs vs air with GHGs) is a simplification: the ~+33 °C jump is the natural greenhouse effect, while present-day air additionally includes a smaller human-enhanced increment. Keep the natural-vs-enhanced distinction explicit so the toggle is not read as showing only the natural effect.
Potency vs abundance reasoning depends on a stated GWP time horizon and gas lifetime; the GWP bars/comparison should specify the time horizon to avoid implying a single fixed 'CH4 vs CO2' ratio.

Comparative efficacy wording ('learners grasp best by…', 'effective for consolidating', 'the reasoning the investigation builds') in the candidate was downgraded to proposed/intended/may language, since no empirical effectiveness has been established for these activities.

Self-audit: the dipole-change criterion, the short-wave/long-wave band assignment, the 255 K / +33 °C / ≈288 K figures, and the natural-vs-enhanced distinction align with the cited ACS material; no arithmetic or physics errors were found requiring correction in learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: Water vapour is a greenhouse gas too. Why does that make it a feedback rather than a direct human 'switch' like CO₂?
Without any natural greenhouse effect Earth would average about −18°C instead of +15°C. So is the greenhouse effect itself the problem, or its enhancement?
Methane is present in far smaller amounts than CO₂ but is called more 'potent.' What does potent mean here?
assess.correctAnswer: The Sun's energy arrives mainly as short-wave radiation, which passes through; Earth's surface warms and re-emits long-wave infrared. Greenhouse-gas molecules (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) have bonds that vibrate at infrared frequencies with a changing dipole, so they absorb and re-emit that outgoing IR; symmetrical N₂ and O₂ have no dipole change when they vibrate, so they don't absorb IR. So greenhouse gases trap outgoing infrared, not incoming sunlight — and it's molecular structure, not abundance, that matters.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Greenhouse gases trap the Sun's heat on its way in / block incoming sunlight'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the two-step model: short-wave in, long-wave IR out, greenhouse gases absorb the OUTGOING IR.
errorPatterns.distractor: They trap the sunlight on its way in to Earth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes trapping of incoming short-wave rather than outgoing IR

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Nitrogen and oxygen trap heat too, just less than CO₂'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Only molecules whose vibration changes their dipole absorb IR; symmetrical N₂/O₂ don't at all.
errorPatterns.distractor: Nitrogen and oxygen trap heat too, just less than CO₂.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: thinks all air gases absorb IR to some degree

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The greenhouse effect is the same thing as the ozone hole'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the mechanisms: greenhouse = trapping outgoing IR; ozone = UV shielding and its depletion.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's the ozone hole letting the heat through.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: conflates IR trapping with ozone depletion

errorPatterns.pattern: 'CO₂ is such a tiny fraction it can't matter'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Potency is IR absorption per molecule, not %; a trace of a strong absorber has a large effect.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: dismisses trace gases on abundance alone

responseLevels.gap: Thinks greenhouse gases block incoming sunlight, that all air gases trap heat, or conflates the effect with the ozone hole.
responseLevels.full: Explains the short-wave-in/long-wave-out model, attributes IR absorption to molecular vibration (dipole change) that symmetrical N₂/O₂ lack, distinguishes natural from enhanced greenhouse effect, and reasons about potency versus abundance — transferring to methane or water vapour.
responseLevels.partial: Knows CO₂/methane trap heat and that the effect can be enhanced, but can't distinguish short-wave in from long-wave out, or can't say why N₂/O₂ don't absorb IR.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The atmosphere is nearly 99% nitrogen and oxygen, yet these gases play almost no part in the greenhouse effect, while CO₂ at under 0.05% does. Why do CO₂ and methane trap heat but nitrogen and oxygen don't — and which radiation are they actually trapping: incoming sunlight, or something else?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who thinks greenhouse gases 'block sunlight coming in,' or that 'more gas = more trapping,' answers differently from one who identifies outgoing IR and the molecular-vibration/dipole reason why only certain molecules absorb it.
